claim: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling patterns embryonic tissues and contributes to homeostasis in adults.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling patterns embryonic tissues and contributes to homeostasis in adults.
evidence: This is a general statement about Hh signaling function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In Drosophila, Hh transport and signaling are thought to occur along a specialized class of actin-rich filopodia, termed cytonemes.
source: In Drosophila, Hh transport and signaling are thought to occur along a specialized class of actin-rich filopodia, termed cytonemes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field, as indicated by the context of the manuscript.

claim: Interference hedgehog (Ihog) forms a Hh receptor complex with Patched to mediate intracellular signaling.
source: Interference hedgehog (Ihog) not only forms a Hh receptor complex with Patched to mediate intracellular signaling, but Ihog also engages in trans-homophilic binding leading to cytoneme stabilization in a manner independent of its role as the Hh receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior knowledge in the field.

claim: Ihog engages in trans-homophilic binding leading to cytoneme stabilization in a manner independent of its role as the Hh receptor.
source: Interference hedgehog (Ihog) not only forms a Hh receptor complex with Patched to mediate intracellular signaling, but Ihog also engages in trans-homophilic binding leading to cytoneme stabilization in a manner independent of its role as the Hh receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Both functions of Ihog (trans-homophilic binding for cytoneme stabilization and Hh binding for ligand sensing) involve a heparin-binding site on the first fibronectin repeat of the extracellular domain.
source: Both functions of Ihog (trans-homophilic binding for cytoneme stabilization and Hh binding for ligand sensing) involve a heparin-binding site on the first fibronectin repeat of the extracellular domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from structure-function analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Ihog-Ihog interaction and the Hh-Ihog interaction cannot occur simultaneously for a single Ihog molecule.
source: Thus, the Ihog-Ihog interaction and the Hh-Ihog interaction cannot occur simultaneously for a single Ihog molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural overlap of binding sites and supported by experimental data.

claim: Hh-Ihog heterophilic interaction dominates over Ihog-Ihog trans-homophilic interaction.
source: By combining experimental data and mathematical modeling, we determined that Hh-Ihog heterophilic interaction dominates and Hh can disrupt and displace Ihog molecules involved in trans-homophilic binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by both experimental data from cell aggregation assays and computational modeling results.

claim: Hh can disrupt and displace Ihog molecules involved in trans-homophilic binding.
source: By combining experimental data and mathematical modeling, we determined that Hh-Ihog heterophilic interaction dominates and Hh can disrupt and displace Ihog molecules involved in trans-homophilic binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Aberration in the precise temporal-spatial regulation and transduction of the Hh signaling pathway is involved in several birth defects.
source: Aberration in the precise temporal-spatial regulation and transduction of the Hh signaling pathway is involved in several birth defects (Muenke and Beachy, 2000) and various proliferative disorders, such as the growth of malignant tumors (Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Aberration in the Hh signaling pathway is involved in various proliferative disorders, such as the growth of malignant tumors.
source: Aberration in the precise temporal-spatial regulation and transduction of the Hh signaling pathway is involved in several birth defects (Muenke and Beachy, 2000) and various proliferative disorders, such as the growth of malignant tumors (Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Hh protein precursor undergoes autoprocessing and lipid modification that generates the mature Hh ligand as an amino-terminal signaling peptide (HhN) dually modified by palmitoyl and cholesteryl adducts.
source: Hh protein precursor undergoes autoprocessing and lipid modification that generates the mature Hh ligand as an amino-terminal signaling peptide (HhN) dually modified by palmitoyl and cholesteryl adducts (Mann and Beachy, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The Hh receptor is comprised of Patched (Ptc) and a member of the Ihog family.
source: The Hh receptor is comprised of Patched (Ptc) and a member of the Ihog family, which in Drosophila is one of the functionally interchangeable proteins encoded by interference Hedgehog (ihog) or brother of ihog (boi) (Lum et al., 2003; McLellan et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006; Camp et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2010; Hartman et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: In Drosophila, the Ihog family consists of functionally interchangeable proteins encoded by interference Hedgehog (ihog) or brother of ihog (boi).
source: The Hh receptor is comprised of Patched (Ptc) and a member of the Ihog family, which in Drosophila is one of the functionally interchangeable proteins encoded by interference Hedgehog (ihog) or brother of ihog (boi) (Lum et al., 2003; McLellan et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006; Camp et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2010; Hartman et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: The first FNIII domain (Fn1) in the extracellular portion of Ihog is involved in binding to the Hh ligand.
source: Previous biochemical and structural studies showed that the first FNIII domain (Fn1) in the extracellular portion of Ihog is involved in binding to the Hh ligand (McLellan et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006), whereas the second FNIII domain (Fn2) of Ihog interacts with Ptc.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The second FNIII domain (Fn2) of Ihog interacts with Ptc.
source: Previous biochemical and structural studies showed that the first FNIII domain (Fn1) in the extracellular portion of Ihog is involved in binding to the Hh ligand (McLellan et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2006), whereas the second FNIII domain (Fn2) of Ihog interacts with Ptc.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Both Fn1 and Fn2 domains are required for Hh signal reception through the formation of a high-affinity multimolecular complex of Ihog, Ptc, and Hh.
source: Both Fn1 and Fn2 domains are required for Hh signal reception through the formation of a high-affinity multimolecular complex of Ihog, Ptc, and Hh (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Ihog proteins mediate cell-cell interactions in a homophilic, calcium-independent manner.
source: Ihog proteins not only play an essential role in Hh signal transduction but also mediate cell-cell interactions in a homophilic, calcium-independent manner (Zheng et al., 2010; Hsia et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The region that mediates the trans Ihog-Ihog interaction overlaps with the region that mediates the interaction with Hh on the Ihog Fn1 domain.
source: The region that mediates the trans Ihog-Ihog interaction overlaps with the region that mediates the interaction with Hh on the Ihog Fn1 domain and includes a region where the negatively charged glycan heparin binds (McLellan et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Heparin is required for Hh-Ihog interactions in vitro.
source: Heparin is required for not only Hh-Ihog interactions but also Ihog-Ihog homophilic trans interactions in vitro (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Heparin is required for Ihog-Ihog homophilic trans interactions in vitro.
source: Heparin is required for not only Hh-Ihog interactions but also Ihog-Ihog homophilic trans interactions in vitro (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Hh is secreted in the posterior (P) compartment and spreads toward the anterior (A) compartment in the Drosophila wing imaginal discs.
source: In the Drosophila wing imaginal discs, Hh is secreted in the posterior (P) compartment and spreads toward the anterior (A) compartment (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Capdevila et al., 1994; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P compartment cells do not express critical components of the Hh pathway, such as the major transcriptional effector Ci.
source: Hh signaling does not occur in P compartment cells because they do not express critical components of the Hh pathway, such as the major transcriptional effector Ci (Eaton and Kornberg, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: A compartment cells can receive and respond to Hh but are unable to produce Hh.
source: In contrast, A compartment cells can receive and respond to Hh but are unable to produce Hh.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila wing disc compartmentalization.

claim: In A compartment cells located close to the source of Hh ligand production at the A/P boundary, Hh signaling triggers pathway activity and an increase in the transcription of target genes.
source: In A compartment cells located close to the source of Hh ligand production at the A/P boundary, Hh signaling triggers pathway activity and, consequently, an increase in the transcription of target genes (Ingham et al., 1991; Basler and Struhl, 1994; Capdevila et al., 1994; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994; Chen and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A model of Hh secretion and transport from the basal surface of the Drosophila wing imaginal discs epithelia involves movement of Hh along cytonemes.
source: A model of Hh secretion and transport from the basal surface of the Drosophila wing imaginal discs epithelia involves movement of Hh along cytonemes (Gradilla et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017), which are dynamic thin cellular protrusions specialized for the intercellular exchange of signaling proteins (Ramírez-Weber and Kornberg, 1999; Roy et al., 2011; Gradilla and Guerrero, 2013; Kornberg, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Cytonemes are dynamic thin cellular protrusions specialized for the intercellular exchange of signaling proteins.
source: A model of Hh secretion and transport from the basal surface of the Drosophila wing imaginal discs epithelia involves movement of Hh along cytonemes (Gradilla et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017), which are dynamic thin cellular protrusions specialized for the intercellular exchange of signaling proteins (Ramírez-Weber and Kornberg, 1999; Roy et al., 2011; Gradilla and Guerrero, 2013; Kornberg, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: When Ihog is co-expressed with the cytoskeletal and membrane markers, thin cellular protrusions are much easier to be detected microscopically.
source: Intriguingly, when Ihog is co-expressed with the cytoskeletal and membrane markers of these structures, these thin cellular protrusions are much easier to be detected microscopically (Callejo et al., 2011; Bilioni et al., 2013; Bischoff et al., 2013; González-Méndez et al., 2017), which suggests that Ihog has roles in generating or stabilizing cytonemes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Overexpressed Ihog is used as a cytoneme marker to visualize these structures.
source: Moreover, overexpressed Ihog is used as a cytoneme marker to visualize these structures (Portela et al., 2019; González-Méndez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Cytonemes with ectopic expression of Ihog were longer with periodic annular structures compared to cytonemes visualized by GMA-GFP.
source: Unlike the short, mostly uniform cytonemes visualized by staining for GMA-GFP, the cytonemes with ectopic expression of Ihog were longer with periodic annular structures (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Annular structures along cytonemes represent stable links between Hh-sending and Hh-receiving cytonemes.
source: These annular structures were proposed to represent stable links between Hh-sending and Hh-receiving cytonemes (González-Méndez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Of the tested Hh components (Hh ligands, Ptc, Dally, and Dlp), only expression of Ihog led to formation of annular structures or increased cytoneme length.
source: Of the tested Hh components, only expression of Ihog lead to formation of the annular structures or increased cytoneme length (Figure 1A-C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the increased frequency of annular structures and length of the cytonemes required Fn1 and an intact heparin-binding surface.
source: These studies revealed that both the increased frequency of annular structures and length of the cytonemes required Fn1 and an intact heparin-binding surface (Figure 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: ptc encodes a component of the Hh receptor and is also a transcriptional target of Hh signaling.
source: ptc not only encodes a component of the Hh receptor but is also a transcriptional target of Hh signaling (Hooper and Scott, 1989; Nakano et al., 1989; Phillips et al., 1990; Capdevila et al., 1994; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The highest expression of ptc is present in a narrow stripe of A cells adjacent to the A/P compartment boundary (Ptchigh).
source: The highest expression of ptc is present in a narrow stripe of A cells adjacent to the A/P compartment boundary (Ptchigh).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ptc expression patterns in the wing disc.

claim: Stabilized cytonemes were observed emanating from Ihog-expressing clones located at the Ptchigh A/P compartment boundary, within the Ptclow A compartment, and Ptcneg P compartment.
source: We observed stabilized cytonemes emanating from with Ihog-expressing clones located not only at the Ptchigh A/P compartment boundary but also within the Ptclow A compartment and Ptcneg P compartment (Figure 2A, upper row).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The cytoneme-stabilizing effect of Ihog was independent of Ptc.
source: Thus, the cytoneme-stabilizing effect of Ihog was independent of Ptc, consistent with the ability of Ihog lacking the Fn2 domain to perform this function (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Expression of Ptc-binding-deficient IhogΔFn2 in the A/P boundary cells resulted in stable cytonemes projecting both posteriorly toward the Hh-secreting P cells and anteriorly away from the Hh source.
source: Moreover, the expression of Ptc-binding-deficient IhogΔFn2 in the A/P boundary cells resulted in stable cytonemes projecting both posteriorly toward the Hh-secreting P cells and anteriorly away from the Hh source (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ihog stabilizes cytonemes through a mechanism different from that used for the formation of Ihog-Ptc receptor complex.
source: These observations indicated that Ihog stabilizes cytonemes through a mechanism different from that used for the formation of Ihog-Ptc receptor complex, which exhibits high-affinity binding to Hh ligands.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Endogenous Hh accumulated along Ihog-overexpressing cytonemes projecting from clones located within the P compartment or from boundary clones projecting posteriorly toward the Hh source.
source: Consistent with Ptc-independent interactions occurring between Ihog and Hh, endogenous Hh accumulated along Ihog-overexpressing cytonemes either projecting from clones located within the P compartment or from boundary clones projecting posteriorly toward the Hh source (Figure 2A, lower row).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No or very little Hh staining was detected with Ihog-expressing cytonemes from clones within the A compartment or with Ihog-expressing cytonemes from clones at the A/P boundary and extending into the A compartment.
source: No or very little Hh staining was detected with Ihog-expressing cytonemes from clones within the A compartment or with Ihog-expressing cytonemes from clones at the A/P boundary and extending into the A compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from immunostaining experiments.

claim: Ihog expression stabilized cytonemes projecting within or toward the A compartment despite the absence or limited amount of Hh ligands.
source: Despite the absence or limited amount of Hh ligands, Ihog expression stabilized all the cytonemes projecting within or toward the A compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the manuscript.

claim: Ihog Fn1-mediated binding to Hh ligands did not account for the stable cytonemes visualized by ectopic Ihog expression in the wing imaginal disc cells.
source: These results indicated that Ihog Fn1-mediated binding to Hh ligands did not account for the stable cytonemes visualized by ectopic Ihog expression in the wing imaginal disc cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing cytoneme stabilization in the absence of Hh.

claim: Cytoneme stabilization by Ihog was independent of position within the wing disc and thus the abundance of Ptc or Hh ligands.
source: Quantification of cytoneme length and the number of annular structures per cytoneme for Ihog-expressing clones in the A compartment, P compartment, and at the boundary showed that cytoneme stabilization by Ihog was independent of position within the wing disc and thus the abundance of Ptc or Hh ligands (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Neither the presence of Ptc nor Hh is necessary for Ihog-mediated cytoneme stabilization.
source: Collectively, our results indicated that neither the presence of Ptc nor Hh is necessary for Ihog-mediated cytoneme stabilization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The function of Ihog in cytoneme stabilization is separate from its function in the Hh receptor complex.
source: This function of Ihog was separate from its function in the Hh receptor complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing Ptc- and Hh-independent cytoneme stabilization.

claim: Endogenous Dlp accumulated along Ihog-expressing cytonemes in the P compartment, along the A/P boundary, and within the A compartment.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we detected a striking accumulation of endogenous Dlp along Ihog-expressing cytonemes not only in the P compartment or along the A/P boundary where both Ihog-Hh and Ihog-Ihog interactions exist (Figure 3A) but also within the A compartment that lacks Hh and where only Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions could occur (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Dlp accumulated along the apical and lateral cell-cell contacts where homophilic Ihog trans binding contributes to cell segregation in the wing imaginal disc epithelium.
source: Additionally, Dlp accumulated along the apical and lateral cell-cell contacts (Figure 3B; yellow outlined regions), where homophilic Ihog trans binding contributes to cell segregation in the wing imaginal disc epithelium (Hsia et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior work.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ihog caused the accumulation of endogenous Dally along the apical and lateral cell-cell contacts and basal cytonemes.
source: We also observed that ectopic expression of Ihog caused the accumulation of endogenous Dally along the apical and lateral cell-cell contacts and basal cytonemes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of neither Dally nor Dlp resulted in cytoneme stabilization in the wing discs.
source: However, ectopic expression of neither Dally nor Dlp resulted in cytoneme stabilization in the wing discs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The roles of Ihog and the glypicans in stabilizing the cytonemes are different.
source: Thus, the roles of Ihog and the glypicans in stabilizing the cytonemes are different.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that glypicans alone do not stabilize cytonemes.

claim: The heparan sulfate chains of Dally or Dlp provide the bridging function in Ihog-Ihog trans interactions.
source: Given the known function of heparin as a bridging molecule in Ihog-Ihog or Ihog-Hh interactions, our results suggested that the heparan sulfate chains of Dally or Dlp provide this function in Ihog-Ihog trans interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and known functions of heparin.

claim: Dlp is distributed in most cells, except in a zone ~7–10 cell diameters in width and centered at the dorsal ventral (D/V) boundary.
source: Dlp is distributed in most cells, except in a zone ~7–10 cell diameters in width and centered at the dorsal ventral (D/V) boundary.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Dlp distribution patterns cited from prior work.

claim: Dally is broadly distributed with highest abundance along the D/V boundary.
source: Dally is also broadly distributed; however, Dally abundance is highest along the D/V boundary (Fujise et al., 2001; Fujise et al., 2003; Han et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Both Dally and Dlp were enriched along the cytonemes and at the apical and lateral cell contacts of Ihog-expressing cells away from the D/V boundary.
source: In agreement with these different distributions, both Dally and Dlp were enriched along the cytonemes and at the apical and lateral cell contacts of Ihog-expressing cells away from the D/V boundary, whereas the Ihog-expressing cells flanking the D/V boundary were positive for Dally with little or no detectable Dlp (Figure 3B, blue outline; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ihog-expressing cells flanking the D/V boundary were positive for Dally with little or no detectable Dlp.
source: In agreement with these different distributions, both Dally and Dlp were enriched along the cytonemes and at the apical and lateral cell contacts of Ihog-expressing cells away from the D/V boundary, whereas the Ihog-expressing cells flanking the D/V boundary were positive for Dally with little or no detectable Dlp (Figure 3B, blue outline; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ihog-mediated homophilic binding occurred in the absence of the Ihog Fn2 domain.
source: Similar to the Ihog-mediated homophilic binding, Ihog-induced Dlp accumulation occurred in the absence of the Ihog Fn2 domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither ectopic expression of IhogΔFn1 nor IhogxHep resulted in the accumulation of Dlp.
source: In contrast, neither ectopic expression of IhogΔFn1 nor IhogxHep, both of which lack homophilic binding capability, resulted in the accumulation of Dlp (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ihog Fn1-mediated homophilic trans interactions, assisted by the heparan sulfate chains of Dally or Dlp, contribute to cytoneme stabilization.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that Ihog Fn1-mediated homophilic trans interactions, assisted by the heparan sulfate chains of Dally or Dlp in the wing imaginal discs, contribute to cytoneme stabilization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ihog in non-adherent Drosophila S2 cells induces cell aggregation via homophilic trans interactions.
source: We previously found that ectopic expression of Ihog in the non-adherent Drosophila S2 cells induces cell aggregation via homophilic trans interactions (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Pairs of Ihog-YFP-positive S2 cells in close contact showed a peak of Ihog-YFP signal along the site of cell-cell contact.
source: Pairs of Ihog-YFP-positive S2 cells in close contact (aggregated) showed a peak of Ihog-YFP signal along the site of cell-cell contact (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C, Figure 4—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Ihog-YFP was enriched in filopodia-like structures on dispersed S2 cells.
source: In contrast, Ihog-YFP was enriched in filopodia-like structures on dispersed S2 cells when evaluated for live cells or fixed cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G, Figure 4—videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: Drosophila S2 cell filopodia recapitulate structural and functional characteristics of cytonemes in the imaginal disc.
source: Because Drosophila S2 cell filopodia recapitulate structural and functional characteristics of cytonemes in the imaginal disc (Bodeen et al., 2017), here, we take advantage of these dispersed Ihog-YFP-expressing S2 cells to evaluate the possibility of filopodia-localized Ihog proteins in participating homophilic trans interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: An Ihog-positive cell extended fewer filopodia toward an Ihog-negative cell compared to filopodia projecting toward another Ihog-positive cell.
source: In contrast, an Ihog-positive cell extend fewer filopodia toward an Ihog-negative cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Two closely positioned Ihog-positive cells exhibited an increase in the number of filopodia oriented toward the nearby Ihog-positive cell.
source: Two closely positioned Ihog-positive cells exhibited an increase in the number of filopodia oriented toward the nearby Ihog-positive cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Filopodia extending from non-adjacent Ihog-YFP-expressing cells interdigitated, then shortened to bring the two cells closer, and finally established a stable cell-cell contact.
source: Moreover, using live-cell time-lapse imaging, we observed that filopodia extending from non-adjacent Ihog-YFP-expressing cells interdigitated, then shortened to bring the two cells closer, and finally established a stable cell-cell contact (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Filopodia-localized Ihog proteins engaged in homophilic trans binding evidenced by the contact initiation along the filopodia of non-adjacent Ihog-expressing S2 cells.
source: Collectively, the observations in S2 cells suggested that filopodia-localized Ihog proteins engaged in homophilic trans binding evidenced by the contact initiation along the filopodia of non-adjacent Ihog-expressing S2 cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations in S2 cells.

claim: Cytonemes projecting from closely positioned Ihog-expressing clones appeared to come into contact.
source: To explore if such events occurred in vivo, we generated Ihog-expressing clones in the wing imaginal discs and found that cytonemes projecting from closely positioned clones appeared to come into contact (Figure 4A; arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wing imaginal disc epithelial cells tightly adhere to their immediate neighbors and maintained stable cell-neighbor relationships.
source: Unlike cultured S2 cells, the wing imaginal disc epithelial cells tightly adhere to their immediate neighbors and maintained stable cell-neighbor relationships (Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Gibson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: GRASP fluorescence was detected both at the lateral cell-cell contacts and along the basal cytonemes of adjacent clones expressing Ihog-RFP plus CD4-spGFP11 or IhogΔFn2-HA plus CD4-spGFP1-10.
source: When these two types of clones were located immediately adjacent to each other, GRASP fluorescence was detected both at the lateral cell-cell contacts and along the basal cytonemes of the adjacent clones expressing Ihog-RFP plus CD4-spGFP11 or IhogΔFn2-HA plus CD4-spGFP1-10 (Figure 4C,D; blue outline and blue arrow).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: GRASP fluorescence appeared along the length of the cytonemes projecting from non-adjacent Ihog-RFP plus CD4-spGFP11 and IhogΔFn2-HA plus CD4-spGFP1-10 expressing cells that do not share common boundaries.
source: Indeed, GRASP fluorescence also appeared along the length of the cytonemes projecting from the non-adjacent Ihog-RFP plus CD4-spGFP11 and IhogΔFn2-HA plus CD4-spGFP1-10 expressing cells that do not share common boundaries as indicated by the lack of GRASP fluorescence throughout the lateral clonal borders (Figure 4C,D; yellow outline and yellow arrow).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Membrane contacts were initiated and established along Ihog-expressing cytonemes.
source: Therefore, the GRASP-marked cytoneme-cytoneme contacts from non-adjacent clones suggested that membrane contacts were initiated and established along Ihog-expressing cytonemes, supporting the idea that Ihog-Ihog trans-binding can occur along opposing cytoneme membranes in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GRASP experimental results.

claim: Ihog-Ihog trans-binding can occur along opposing cytoneme membranes in vivo.
source: Therefore, the GRASP-marked cytoneme-cytoneme contacts from non-adjacent clones suggested that membrane contacts were initiated and established along Ihog-expressing cytonemes, supporting the idea that Ihog-Ihog trans-binding can occur along opposing cytoneme membranes in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GRASP experimental results.

claim: Cytoneme length correlated with the number of cytoneme-cytoneme interaction events (Pearson r = 0.7939).
source: Thus, the simulations indicated that cytoneme length correlated with the number of cytoneme-cytoneme interaction events (Figure 5D, Pearson r = 0.7939).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Average cytoneme length increased with stronger cytoneme-cytoneme interactions.
source: By varying the strength of homophilic trans interactions, we also found that average cytoneme length increased with stronger cytoneme-cytoneme interactions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The cytoneme bundling index increased as the strength of the homophilic trans interactions among cytonemes increased.
source: The cytoneme bundling index increased as the strength of the homophilic trans interactions among cytonemes increased (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Thin cytonemes appeared to form thick bundles in Ihog-expressing wing disc cells when imaged with Airyscan technology.
source: Consistent with the computational modeling prediction, we detected thin cytonemes (Figure 5G, blue arrows) that appeared to form thick bundles (Figure 5G, red arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G using Airyscan imaging.

claim: Cytoneme bundling was rarely observed upon expression of only the membrane marker GPI-YFP or expression of the homophilic binding-deficient Ihog variants IhogΔFn1 and IhogxHep.
source: In contrast, we rarely observed cytoneme bundling upon expression of only the membrane marker GPI-YFP or expression of the homophilic binding-deficient Ihog variants IhogΔFn1 and IhogxHep (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Trans Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions increase cytoneme length and bundling.
source: Taken together, our in vivo and in silico studies showed that trans Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions increase cytoneme length and bundling (Figures 1–5), which in turn explained why the cytonemes expressing ectopic Ihog proteins were much easier to be detected microscopically and Ihog was often used as a cytoneme marker to visualize these structures (Callejo et al., 2011; Bilioni et al., 2013; Bischoff et al., 2013; González-Méndez et al., 2017; Portela et al., 2019; González-Méndez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by both experimental data and computational modeling results.

claim: Large cytoneme bundles were only observed when Ihog was overexpressed, and physiological amounts of Ihog were not sufficient to promote extensive bundling of cytonemes detectable under regular or Airyscan confocal microscope.
source: It is also worth noting, the large cytoneme bundles were only observed when Ihog was overexpressed, and physiological amounts of Ihog were not sufficient to promote extensive bundling of cytonemes detectable under regular or Airyscan confocal microscope (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in multiple figures.

claim: Knockdown of ihog in the absence of boi resulted in cytonemes with significantly reduced length compared to cytonemes in boi mutant animals retaining normal amounts of Ihog.
source: Nevertheless, consistent with the finding that ectopic Ihog leads to elongated cytonemes, knockdown of ihog in the absence of its close paralog-encoding gene boi resulted in cytonemes with significantly reduced length compared with the length of cytonemes in boi mutant animals retaining normal amounts of Ihog (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Endogenous Ihog proteins play a crucial role in regulating the structure of cytonemes through Ihog-mediated cytoneme-cytoneme interactions.
source: Therefore, endogenous Ihog proteins also played a crucial role in regulating the structure of cytonemes, which our data indicated involved Ihog-mediated cytoneme-cytoneme interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced cytoneme length upon ihog knockdown.

claim: The dissociation constant for the nonlipid-modified recombinant HhN and the extracellular portion of Ihog containing the Fn1 and Fn2 domains (IhogFn1-2), measured in solution, is ~2 μM.
source: The dissociation constant for the nonlipid-modified recombinant HhN and the extracellular portion of Ihog containing the Fn1 and Fn2 domains (IhogFn1-2), measured in solution, is ~2 μM (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Soluble HhN at 30 μM competes for Ihog homophilic interactions in a pull-down assay in which HhN and Ihog are mixed simultaneously.
source: Additionally, soluble HhN at 30 μM competes for Ihog homophilic interactions in a pull-down assay in which HhN and Ihog are mixed simultaneously (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Soluble HhN at 30 µM had little effect on Ihog-mediated cell aggregation.
source: Unexpectedly, even at 30 µM, a concentration 10 times higher than the reported IhogFn12-HhN dissociation constant, soluble HhN had little effect on Ihog-mediated cell aggregation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Soluble HhN does not reach a sufficiently high concentration at the cell surface to compete for the extensive homophilic trans interactions that can be mediated by membrane-tethered Ihog proteins.
source: One explanation is that soluble HhN does not reach a sufficiently high concentration at the cell surface to compete for the extensive homophilic trans interactions that can be mediated by membrane-tethered Ihog proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lack of effect of soluble HhN on cell aggregation.

claim: Expression of cDNA encoding full-length Hh in S2 cells generates dually lipid-modified Hh ligands.
source: Expression of cDNA encoding full-length Hh in S2 cells generates dually lipid-modified Hh ligands, whereas expressing cDNA encoding the amino-terminal signaling fragment results in HhN lacking a cholesterol modification (Burke et al., 1999; Porter et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Expressing cDNA encoding the amino-terminal signaling fragment results in HhN lacking a cholesterol modification.
source: Expression of cDNA encoding full-length Hh in S2 cells generates dually lipid-modified Hh ligands, whereas expressing cDNA encoding the amino-terminal signaling fragment results in HhN lacking a cholesterol modification (Burke et al., 1999; Porter et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Both forms of Hh ligands (dually lipid-modified and HhN lacking cholesterol) are competent to bind to the receptors and induce Hh signaling in ligand-receiving cells.
source: Although both forms of Hh ligands are competent to bind to the receptors and induce Hh signaling in ligand-receiving cells, HhN does not require Dispatched (Disp) for release from the producing cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hh ligand forms and their signaling competence.

claim: HhN does not require Dispatched (Disp) for release from the producing cell.
source: Although both forms of Hh ligands are competent to bind to the receptors and induce Hh signaling in ligand-receiving cells, HhN does not require Dispatched (Disp) for release from the producing cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HhN release mechanisms.

claim: In S2 cells without ectopically expressing Disp, only dually lipid-modified Hh ligands, but not HhN lacking a cholesterol modification, was associated with the membrane of the transfected cells.
source: Thus, in S2 cells without also ectopically expressing Disp, only dually lipid-modified Hh ligands, but not HhN lacking a cholesterol modification, was associated with the membrane of the transfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hh-expressing cells aggregated when mixed with Ihog-expressing cells.
source: We found that Hh-expressing cells, which did not aggregate by themselves (Figure 6A, mCherry+Hh, GFP+Hh), aggregated when mixed with Ihog-expressing cells (Figure 6A, mCherry+Ihog, GFP+Hh).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HhN-expressing cells neither aggregated themselves nor with Ihog-expressing cells.
source: In contrast, HhN-expressing cells neither aggregated themselves (Figure 6A, mCherry+HhN, GFP+HhN) nor with Ihog-expressing cells (Figure 6A, mCherry+Ihog, GFP+HhN).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Aggregates formed by cells expressing Hh with GFP and cells expressing Ihog with mCherry exhibited a checkerboard-like pattern with evenly distributed red and green cells.
source: We observed a checkerboard-like pattern with evenly distributed red and green cells in aggregates formed by cells expressing Hh with GFP and cells expressing Ihog with mCherry (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In aggregates of Hh- and Ihog-expressing cells, most center cells had four or five neighbors, and cells expressing the same transfected proteins ('like' cells) were rare among those neighbors.
source: Most center cells within the cell aggregates had four or five neighbors (Figure 6C). Furthermore, among those neighbors, cells expressing the same transfected proteins and thus of the same color ('like' cell) were rare (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: Aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells labeled with either GFP or mCherry exhibited a honeycomb pattern.
source: In contrast, aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells labeled with either GFP or mCherry exhibited a honeycomb pattern (Figure 6B): Most center cells had five or six neighbors (Figure 6C), and ~50% were 'like' cells (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: In aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells, most center cells had five or six neighbors, and ~50% were 'like' cells.
source: In contrast, aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells labeled with either GFP or mCherry exhibited a honeycomb pattern (Figure 6B): Most center cells had five or six neighbors (Figure 6C), and ~50% were 'like' cells (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: The different cellular patterns formed by cells expressing Hh and cells expressing Ihog versus those formed by differentially labeled Ihog-expressing cells suggested that the heterophilic interaction between Ihog and Hh is stronger than the homophilic trans interaction between Ihog proteins on an opposing cell surface.
source: Therefore, the different cellular patterns formed by cells expressing Hh and cells expressing Ihog versus those formed by differentially labeled Ihog-expressing cells suggested that the heterophilic interaction between Ihog and Hh is stronger than the homophilic trans interaction between Ihog proteins on an opposing cell surface.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of different aggregation patterns.

claim: The relative affinity of the Ihog-Hh heterotypic interaction is at least ~20–30 times higher than that of the Ihog-Ihog homotypic trans interaction.
source: Therefore, the neighbor cell analysis from the experimental aggregation assay and the computational modeling suggested that the relative affinity of the Ihog-Hh heterotypic interaction is at least ~ 20–30 times higher than that of the Ihog-Ihog homotypic trans interaction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from both experimental data and computational modeling results.

claim: The dimerization constants for the extracellular portion of Ihog comprising Fn1–2 range from 60 to 430 μM.
source: Previous sedimentation velocity and sedimentation equilibrium experiments predicted that the dimerization constants for the extracellular portion of Ihog comprising Fn1–2 range from 60 to 430 μM and that the dissociation constants for the interaction between HhN and this IhogFn1–2 region were between 0.4 and 8.0 μM (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The dissociation constants for the interaction between HhN and IhogFn1–2 were between 0.4 and 8.0 μM.
source: Previous sedimentation velocity and sedimentation equilibrium experiments predicted that the dimerization constants for the extracellular portion of Ihog comprising Fn1–2 range from 60 to 430 μM and that the dissociation constants for the interaction between HhN and this IhogFn1–2 region were between 0.4 and 8.0 μM (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The modeling prediction of an affinity for the Ihog-Hh heterotypic interaction that is at least 20 times higher than that for the Ihog-Ihog homotypic trans interaction is consistent with the values obtained in biochemical experiments.
source: Although IhogFn1-2 dimerization in vitro could occur both in cis and in trans (McLellan et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2019), our modeling prediction of an affinity for the Ihog-Hh heterotypic interaction that is at least 20 times higher than that for the Ihog-Ihog homotypic trans interaction is consistent with the values obtained in the biochemical experiments (McLellan et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim compares computational modeling predictions with prior biochemical data.

claim: Mixing Hh-expressing cells with pre-existing aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells would displace the relatively weaker Ihog-mediated homophilic interactions by establishing stronger Hh-Ihog interactions and result in a checkerboard pattern.
source: Thus, from our computational analysis of interaction strength, we predicted that mixing Hh-expressing cells with pre-existing aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells would displace the relatively weaker Ihog-mediated homophilic interactions by establishing stronger Hh-Ihog interactions and result in a checkerboard pattern.
evidence: This is a prediction based on computational modeling and differential adhesion theory.

claim: Within 30 min after mixing Hh-expressing cells with preformed aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells, Hh-expressing cells were found on the surface of the pre-existing aggregates.
source: Within 30 min after cell mixing, Hh-expressing cells were found on the surface of the pre-existing aggregates of Ihog-expressing cells, which we interpreted as Hh binding to Ihog proteins that were not engaged in homophilic adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from time-lapse experiments.

claim: By 12 hr after mixing Hh-expressing cells with Ihog-expressing cell aggregates, all cell aggregates contained similar numbers of Hh-expressing cells and Ihog-expressing cells arranged in a checkerboard-like pattern.
source: Over time, Hh-expressing cells were found inside the Ihog-expressing cell aggregates, such that, by 12 hr after mixing, all cell aggregates contained similar numbers of Hh-expressing cells and Ihog-expressing cells arranged in a checkerboard-like pattern (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The observed cellular rearrangement indicated the Hh ligand disrupts trans Ihog-Ihog binding by competing for the Ihog Fn1 domain.
source: Moreover, the observed cellular rearrangement indicated the Hh ligand disrupts trans Ihog-Ihog binding by competing for the Ihog Fn1 domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of cell rearrangement.

claim: Hh binding to Ihog is dominant over Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions and effectively competes for Ihog even in the context of pre-established Ihog-Ihog trans-homophilic interactions.
source: Taken together, these results suggested Hh binding to Ihog is dominant over Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions and effectively competes for Ihog even in the context of pre-established Ihog-Ihog trans-homophilic interactions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental and computational results.

claim: The Ihog homophilic binding site overlaps with Ihog-Hh interface on Fn1 of the Ihog extracellular domain, resulting in competition between Hh binding and Ihog-Ihog trans homophilic interactions.
source: However, the Ihog homophilic binding site overlaps with Ihog-Hh interface on Fn1 of the Ihog extracellular domain, resulting in competition between Hh binding and Ihog-Ihog trans homophilic interactions.
evidence: This is a key finding of the manuscript supported by structural and functional data.

claim: Ihog-Ihog trans interactions promote and stabilize direct cytoneme-cytoneme contacts to facilitate Ihog in reaching and capturing the Hh ligands secreted from the cytonemes.
source: On the basis of these two functions competing for an overlapping surface on the Ihog Fn1 domain and the differential interaction strength between Ihog-Hh heterophilic and Ihog-Ihog trans-homophilic bindings, we propose a model in which Ihog-Ihog trans interactions promote and stabilize direct cytoneme-cytoneme contacts to facilitate Ihog in reaching and capturing the Hh ligands secreted from the cytonemes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The stronger ligand-receptor interaction releases Ihog from the weaker trans-homophilic interaction, enabling the receptor-ligand complex to freely transport or become internalized along the cytonemes.
source: The stronger ligand-receptor interaction releases Ihog from the weaker trans-homophilic interaction, enabling the receptor-ligand complex to freely transport or become internalized along the cytonemes.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The apparently incompatible functions of Ihog in homophilic adhesion and ligand binding cooperate to promote Hh transport and reception along the cytonemes.
source: Thus, the apparently incompatible functions of Ihog in homophilic adhesion and ligand binding cooperate to promote Hh transport and reception along the cytonemes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on all the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The affinity of Hh for the Ihog-Ptc receptor complex is higher than the affinity of Hh for the co-receptor Ihog alone.
source: Our model is also consistent with the reported affinity of Hh for the Ihog-Ptc receptor complex, which is higher than the affinity of Hh for the co-receptor Ihog alone (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The presence of Ptc in the Hh-receiving cytoneme is critical to Hh reception in the responding cells.
source: Indeed, the presence of Ptc in the Hh-receiving cytoneme is critical to Hh reception in the responding cells (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The integration of the functions of Ihog depends on the differential affinity (Ihog-Ihog < Ihog-Hh < Ptc-Ihog-Hh) and the competitive binding between Ihog for itself (in trans) and Hh.
source: Thus, we propose that the integration of the functions of Ihog — promotion of cytoneme-cytoneme contacts, Hh delivery, and Hh signal reception — depends on the differential affinity (Ihog-Ihog < Ihog-Hh < Ptc-Ihog-Hh) and the competitive binding between Ihog for itself (in trans) and Hh (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: Both Hh release and cytoneme formation occur at the basal side of the wing disc epithelium.
source: Notably, both Hh release and cytoneme formation occurs at the basal side of the wing disc epithelium (Callejo et al., 2011; Bilioni et al., 2013; Bischoff et al., 2013; Gradilla et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017), making weaker Ihog-Ihog trans interactions accessible for replacement by stronger Ihog-Hh interactions along the cytonemes, where Ihog also functions as the receptor for Hh transport and reception (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Farther from the source of secreted Hh, heterophilic Ihog-Hh interactions would be infrequent along the lateral side of epithelia, where the trans Ihog-Ihog interactions play essential roles in modulating A/P cell segregation and lineage restriction.
source: In contrast, farther from the source of secreted Hh, heterophilic Ihog-Hh interactions would be infrequent along the lateral side of epithelia, where the trans Ihog-Ihog interactions play essential roles in modulating A/P cell segregation and lineage restriction (Hsia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim combines inference from the model with citation to prior work.

claim: Direct membrane contacts are much more extensive along the lateral sides of epithelia compared with that formed along cytonemes.
source: In addition, direct membrane contacts are much more extensive along the lateral sides of epithelia compared with that formed along cytonemes (Figure 5), favoring persistent Ihog-Ihog trans interactions that create an additional barrier for direct competition from the basally released Hh ligands.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions along the cytonemes are readily switchable, whereas those at the lateral cell-cell junctions are more stable and less likely to be disrupted.
source: Thus, in agreement with the functional needs and the availability of Hh ligands, Ihog-Ihog homophilic trans interactions along the cytonemes are readily switchable, whereas those at the lateral cell-cell junctions are more stable and less likely to be disrupted (Figure 8).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions could occur both in trans and in cis.
source: Of note, Ihog-Ihog homophilic interactions could occur both in trans and in cis (McLellan et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The Ihog-mediated homophilic cis interaction was observed in the HhN/IhogFn1–2 crystal structure (PDBID Code 2IBG).
source: The Ihog-mediated homophilic cis interaction was observed in the HhN/IhogFn1–2 crystal structure (PDBID Code 2IBG), in which each HhN molecule contacts a single Ihog molecule, and a pair of 1:1 Hh/Ihog complexes form a dimeric 2:2 complex that is entirely mediated by cis interactions between the IhogFn1 domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: In the HhN/IhogFn1–2 crystal structure, Hh does not interfere with the cis Ihog-Ihog interaction.
source: In this complex, Hh does not interfere with the cis Ihog-Ihog interaction (McLellan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The Ihog-Ihog trans interaction was not revealed in the HhN/IhogFn1–2 crystal structure, likely due to competitive binding by HhN to the heparin-binding surface of IhogFn1 required to establish the trans Ihog-Ihog interaction.
source: In contrast, the Ihog-Ihog trans interaction was not revealed in the HhN/IhogFn1–2 crystal structure, likely due to competitive binding by HhN to the heparin-binding surface of IhogFn1 required to establish the trans Ihog-Ihog interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and the known binding requirements.

claim: HhN-mediated disruption of Ihog-Ihog binding was partial even when the concentration of HhN was 10–15 times higher than the reported dissociation constant of IhogFn1-2 for HhN.
source: Nevertheless, we previously noticed, in an in vitro competitive binding assay, that HhN-mediated disruption of Ihog-Ihog binding was partial even when the concentration of HhN was 10–15 times higher than the reported dissociation constant of IhogFn1-2 for HhN (Wu et al., 2019), suggesting the co-existence of HhN-replaceable trans Ihog-Ihog binding and HhN-irreplaceable cis Ihog-Ihog binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The cis Ihog-Ihog interaction likely can occur in the context of either trans Ihog-Ihog or Ihog-Hh interactions.
source: Thus, the cis Ihog-Ihog interaction likely can occur in the context of either trans Ihog-Ihog or Ihog-Hh interactions (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: Cytoneme-mediated Hh reception and transport have been described in Drosophila abdominal and female germline stem cell niche.
source: Besides the wing imaginal disc epithelia, cytoneme-mediated Hh reception and transport have been described in other Drosophila tissues, such as the abdominal and the female germline stem cell niche (Rojas-Ríos et al., 2012; Bischoff et al., 2013; González-Méndez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The involvement of cytonemes in Hh signaling has been extended from insect to vertebrates by studies of the limb bud of chick embryo and cultured mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: The involvement of cytonemes in Hh signaling has been extended from insect to vertebrates by studies of the limb bud of chick embryo and cultured mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Sanders et al., 2013; Hall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The vertebrate homologs of the Drosophila Ihog proteins, Cdo and Boc, localize in cytonemes.
source: The vertebrate homologs of the Drosophila Ihog proteins, Cdo and Boc, localize in cytonemes, and overexpression of either CDO or BOC increases the number of cytonemes detected on mammalian cells (Hall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Overexpression of either CDO or BOC increases the number of cytonemes detected on mammalian cells.
source: The vertebrate homologs of the Drosophila Ihog proteins, Cdo and Boc, localize in cytonemes, and overexpression of either CDO or BOC increases the number of cytonemes detected on mammalian cells (Hall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Cytonemes have been implicated in the delivery of other paracrine signaling molecules important in development, including Notch, epidermal growth factor, fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein, and Wnt.
source: Moreover, cytonemes have been implicated in the delivery of other paracrine signaling molecules important in development, including Notch, epidermal growth factor, fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein, and Wnt (González-Méndez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Cytonemes from a single cell often exhibit different receptor compositions such that different cytonemes from the same cell can selectively respond to ligands for a specific pathway and not others.
source: Remarkably, cytonemes from a single cell often exhibit different receptor compositions such that different cytonemes from the same cell can selectively respond to ligands for a specific pathway and not others (Roy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.
